details.actual: What block-by-block observations reveal about an uneven summerAma Osei & Milan Shah·2024Urban Field Notes·7 min read·pp. 12–29

What block-by-block observations reveal about an uneven summerAma Osei & Milan Shah·2024Urban Field Notes·7 min read·pp. 12–29At a glanceRepeated walks through six contrasting neighborhoods show why a citywide temperature cannot describe the heat a person actually encounters. Exposure shifts with shade, surfaces, waiting time, and the route available to a walker.“The useful unit of heat exposure is often a journey, not a weather station.”In this notebookSupports the notebook’s distinction between average air temperature and the lived experience of moving through a city.THE FULL TEXT3 sections01A city measured in short walksThe field team followed twelve walking routes through six neighborhoods during three periods of a hot day. Each route linked an everyday origin and destination: a home and a bus stop, a school and a shop, or a clinic and a public square. At regular intervals, observers recorded shade, pavement condition, wind, and the places where people stopped. The purpose was to describe a sequence of exposures rather than to assign a single temperature to an entire neighborhood.Conditions changed over distances that conventional city maps treat as negligible. A shaded side street could lead directly into an exposed intersection. A bus shelter offered a roof but little protection from the low afternoon sun. One small courtyard remained comfortable long after the adjacent sidewalk became difficult to occupy. These transitions mattered because walkers could not always choose a different route or travel at a different time.Measurements were paired with route diaries. Participants described where they slowed down, crossed the street for shade, or chose to wait indoors. The diaries made it possible to separate a place that was briefly uncomfortable from a place that interrupted a necessary trip. A short exposed section near a clinic had greater practical significance than a larger hot area that most participants could avoid.02The limits of a neighborhood averageA neighborhood mean can conceal both useful refuges and concentrated burdens. The field observations did not suggest abandoning broad temperature maps; they showed that those maps answer a different question. An average helps identify where investment may be needed. A route-level account helps determine what that investment should change for someone leaving home on a hot afternoon.Shade was most valuable where it coincided with unavoidable waiting. Crossings, transit stops, school gates, and clinic entrances emerged repeatedly in the diaries. A tree canopy elsewhere in the same block did not compensate for an exposed waiting area if the person could not leave the queue. Spatial proximity was therefore an incomplete measure of access.The team also observed a timing problem. A street that appeared well shaded in the morning could become exposed during the hours when school pickup and errands were most common. A useful public map would show how protection changes during the day, or at least identify the period represented by each observation.03From observations to decisionsThe report recommends combining repeated walks with a small set of resident-defined routes. This approach keeps the work manageable while preserving the relationship between an intervention and the activity it supports. The question becomes whether a person can reach the bus, buy groceries, or visit a neighbor with fewer difficult stretches along the way.The authors caution that the study covers a limited set of weather conditions and does not establish health outcomes. Its contribution is a practical method for noticing exposure that can disappear in aggregate data. Repeating the walks after a shade or pavement intervention would provide an immediate, legible account of what changed and what remains unresolved.Source detailsPublishedJune 18, 2024Pages12–29Osei, A., & Shah, M. Nighttime heat, housing, and the recovery hours between hot daysElena Rivera & Noah Bell·2025Built Environment Working Papers·8 min read·pp. 1–22

Nighttime heat, housing, and the recovery hours between hot daysElena Rivera & Noah Bell·2025Built Environment Working Papers·8 min read·pp. 1–22At a glanceInterviews and indoor observations explore how warm nights extend the effects of a hot day. The paper connects building conditions with household choices and asks how public heat responses can account for the hours after sunset.“Sunset changes the light before it changes the conditions inside a home.”In this notebookBroadens the notebook beyond outdoor daytime routes to the continuity of exposure and the importance of overnight recovery.THE FULL TEXT3 sections01The hours after sunsetPublic descriptions of heat often focus on the afternoon peak. Residents interviewed for this working paper described a different boundary: the point at which their homes became comfortable enough to rest. On some nights, that point arrived well after midnight. On others, it did not arrive before the next day began. The authors use these accounts to examine the continuity between daytime exposure and nighttime recovery.The study paired indoor observations with interviews in a varied group of homes. Its purpose was exploratory rather than representative. The records show how building orientation, stored heat, ventilation options, and household routines interacted over several consecutive warm days. Rooms with similar daytime readings sometimes cooled at very different rates after sunset.The household accounts also show why opening a window is not a simple or universal response. Noise, outdoor air conditions, insects, privacy, and concerns about security all influenced whether residents felt able to ventilate their homes. These constraints were particularly important for people whose bedrooms faced busy streets or shared outdoor spaces.02Heat moves through a household routineParticipants described moving meals to a different room, postponing chores that generated heat, or changing where family members slept. These adaptations required space, time, and coordination. A household with several rooms had options that a household in a single small space did not. The apparent simplicity of an adaptation therefore concealed differences in the resources needed to carry it out.Warm nights affected the following day’s choices. Some residents postponed errands after poor sleep. Others left home early to spend time in a cooler public building, changing the hours in which transport and public facilities were most useful. The paper suggests that services planned only around the hottest afternoon period may miss these changes in routine.The authors distinguish immediate coping from durable improvement. A fan or a temporary cool room may provide practical relief, while building repairs and changes to the surrounding environment address conditions over a longer period. The two forms of response operate on different timescales and should be considered together.03Connecting the home and the neighborhoodThe paper argues that a heat response should connect indoor and outdoor conditions. An evening public space may be useful only if it is comfortable to reach and remains open when residents need it. Advice about ventilation should reflect the conditions outside the window. Information about services should be clear enough to use when people are tired and routines have already been disrupted.The findings are limited by the small sample and the short observation period. They do not establish a single building solution or a clinical threshold. Their value is to describe the hours that disappear when a heat event is represented only by a daytime maximum, and to identify questions for a more sustained study of recovery between hot days.Source detailsPublishedFebruary 12, 2025Pages1–22Rivera, E., & Bell, N.
